# React

- Function components with hooks. Every hook is declared before any conditional `return`; hooks run in the same order every render. `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` and `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` are errors.
- Server state lives in TanStack Query, and only there. Each resource has one module of query keys and hooks (`useTasks`, `useUpdateTask`); components never build query keys inline. Mutations that the user should see at once (reorder, toggle, delete) are optimistic, roll back on error and show the error.
- `useState` is for local affordances only: an open menu, a draft form value. Auth state is one context. Never copy server data into local state.
- Derive, do not mirror. A value computed from props or query data is computed during render (with `useMemo` only when it is measurably costly), never stored by an effect. `useEffect` is for syncing with something outside React, not for data flow.
- Forms validate with the same Zod schema the API layer uses, and show errors next to the field.
- Responsive by default, mobile first: Tailwind utilities, layouts that work from 320px wide up, touch targets of at least 44px, reorder that works by touch and by keyboard as well as by mouse.
- Accessible by default: real buttons and links, a label on every input, visible focus, and roles and names that tests query by.
- Styling: Tailwind utilities first. Inline `style` only for values the utility layer cannot express.
# Testing

Robust testing is a hard requirement, and so is test-driven development. Applies to every change.

## Test first
- Red, green, refactor. Write the test, run it and watch it fail for the expected reason, write the least code that makes it pass, then clean up with the test still green. Run the red step in the session so the transcript shows it.
- Every commit is green. All suites that the change touches pass before `git commit`; a failing test is never committed. A commit holds the test and the code that passes it together.
- New behaviour gets a test in the same commit. A bug fix starts with a test that reproduces the bug.

## Each layer earns its place
Test a behaviour once, at the lowest layer that can catch it. A higher layer covers only what the lower layers cannot see. Before adding a test, name the failure it catches that no existing test catches; if there is none, do not add it.

| Layer | Tool | Owns | Does not re-test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backend unit | pytest | pure functions in the core: ordering, search filters, validation, token and password helpers | anything HTTP or SQL |
| Backend integration | pytest, httpx `ASGITransport`, a real database | each endpoint's contract: status codes, response shape, auth, ownership, persistence | the pure rules already unit-tested, beyond one case that proves the wiring |
| Frontend unit and component | Vitest (its API matches Jest's), React Testing Library, MSW at the `fetch` boundary | pure helpers, hooks, and each screen's states: loading, empty, error, success, validation | backend rules |
| Live-server e2e | pytest against the running stack (compose, then k3d) | what only a deployed stack shows: migrations ran, the proxy and cookie path, ingress and routing, a session issued by one replica accepted by another | endpoint contracts |
| Browser e2e | Playwright against the running stack | a few complete user journeys: sign in, create, reorder, search, edit, delete, sign out; and the small-screen layout | screen states and endpoint contracts |
| Load | k6 from its container against the running stack | latency and error budgets at 200 concurrent users, data consistency afterwards, and the round's capacity figure from a stepped run | correctness of single requests |

## Concurrency
- Each race in the spec has an integration test named after it that fires the requests together with `asyncio.TaskGroup` against a real Postgres. Each one must fail when its guard is removed; show that once, in the session.
- A fixture runs the backend suite in asyncio debug mode with a 50 ms slow-callback threshold and fails any test during which the event loop was blocked.
- The race tests and the load tests are run with the lead present: show the scripts and budgets first, then walk through the results.

## Mechanics
- Mock at the boundary (the HTTP client, `fetch`, the clock), never inside the code under test. Nothing in a unit suite opens a socket.
- Tests are independent and order-free. Each builds its own data through factories or fixtures; none relies on another's leftovers.
- Assert on behaviour a user or caller can see: status, body, rendered text and roles. Never on private attributes or CSS class names.
- One reason to fail per test. The name says the behaviour: `test_reorder_rejects_task_owned_by_another_user`, `it("shows the empty state when the user has no tasks")`.
- Coverage is a floor, not a target: CI fails below the threshold set in `pyproject.toml` and `vitest.config.ts`. A line covered by a test that asserts nothing is not covered.
- Report results as they are. "128 passed" means you saw it. Name the suite and the stack it ran against.
# Coding standards

Applies to `backend/` (Python) and `frontend/` (TypeScript). The path-scoped rules add the language detail.

## General
- Minimal code. No speculative abstractions. No options nobody asked for.
- Concise but descriptive. A name says what a thing is or does; a reader should not need the comment to follow the code.
- Prefer editing an existing file to adding one. Delete what is unused. No dead branches.
- Every public function, class, component and type carries a one-line summary in the language's doc format (Google-style docstrings in Python, JSDoc in TypeScript). Sections (`Args:`, `@param`) only when they add something the signature does not say. Other comments are single line and only where the code cannot say it. No comment blocks. No commented-out code.
- Every change is verifiable. If you cannot test it, say so before shipping it.
- Match the surrounding code's style, not its gaps.

## Functional and declarative style (a hard requirement)
- Functional core, imperative shell. Domain logic (validation, ordering, search filters, mapping rows to responses) is pure functions with no I/O. Routers, repositories and React components are the thin shell that does I/O and calls the core.
- Never mutate an input. Return a new value. Python: frozen dataclasses, Pydantic models with `frozen=True` where they flow through the core, tuples over lists for fixed data. TypeScript: `const`, `readonly`, spread, `toSorted`/`toSpliced`/`with` over `sort`/`splice`.
- Prefer expressions to statements: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, comprehensions and generator expressions over loops that append into an accumulator. Use a loop only when it reads more clearly, and never just to mutate an outer variable.
- Compose small functions instead of writing one long one. Higher-order functions where they remove repetition: FastAPI `Depends` factories, decorators, hooks that take a query function, comparator builders. Do not add one for a single caller.
- Pick the data structure for the access pattern: a dict or `Map` for lookup by id, a set for membership, a list or tuple for order. Say why in review when it is not obvious.
- No hidden shared mutable state: no module-level caches that requests write to, no singletons holding request data.

## Async and concurrency (a hard requirement)
- Use the high-level abstraction, never hand-rolled threads or callbacks. Backend: `async def` handlers, the async SQLAlchemy session, `asyncio.TaskGroup` (or `gather`) when independent awaits can run together. Frontend: TanStack Query for all server state (caching, retries, cancellation, optimistic updates with rollback), never `useEffect` plus `fetch`.
- Never block the event loop. CPU-heavy work (password hashing) runs through `asyncio.to_thread` or the library's async API.

## Boundaries and types
- Every value that crosses a boundary (HTTP body, database row, token claims, storage, URL params) is a typed model, validated right after it is read: Pydantic in Python, Zod in TypeScript. Field access happens on the validated value. No `dict[str, Any]`, `any` or `Record<string, unknown>` for a known shape.
- Type hints on every parameter and return value, tests included. TypeScript is `strict`; no `any`, no `as unknown as`, no `@ts-ignore`.

## Logging
- Logs exist to monitor the running app and find bugs. Keep every line that does that: startup and ready, shutdown, a caught exception with its context, a request that failed auth or validation at WARNING, a degraded path taken.
- Remove every line added only to chase a bug during development before the commit. A log line that would not help someone on call is noise.
- Backend: `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)`, never `print`. Frontend: `console.info` for lifecycle, `console.warn` and `console.error` for failures; never `console.log` or `console.debug`. ESLint enforces the frontend list.
- WARNING and ERROR lines say where, why and what happens next, with ids as key=value (`user_id=`, `task_id=`, `request_id=`). Never log secrets, passwords, tokens or full request bodies.

## Hygiene
- No `TODO`, `FIXME`, `XXX` or `HACK` in code. A follow-up goes in the PR description or an issue.
- No `debugger`, `breakpoint()`, `pdb`, or focused tests (`.only`). `python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py` checks all of this and runs in CI and in `/verify`.
- Secrets never appear in code, logs, tests, or chat. `.env` files and key material are off limits; a hook enforces this. Anything bundled into the frontend is public.
# Git and pull requests

## Branches
- Work on a branch off `main`: `feature/<name>`, `fix/<name>`, `chore/<name>`, `docs/<name>`, `refactor/<name>`, `perf/<name>`, `test/<name>`, `ci/<name>`. Lowercase, hyphens, no personal names.
- Never commit on `main`. Never force-push a shared branch. Never `--no-verify`. A hook blocks all three.
- Releases are `vX.Y.Z` tags on `main`. A tag is never moved or deleted; a wrong tag is fixed by cutting the next version. A hook blocks tag moves.

## Commits
- One logical change per commit, and every commit is green (see `testing.md`). Conventional Commits: `type(scope): subject`. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert, release. Scopes: `api`, `web`, `db`, `auth`, `deploy`, `claude`, or none. Subject starts lowercase, no trailing period, imperative mood.
- The body says why, not what.
- Add `Refs: #<issue>` or `Refs: docs/plans/<file>.md` when there is one.

## Pull requests
- Run `/raise-pr`. It shows the card (title, branch, base, assignee, label, summary) and waits for a yes.
- The title follows the commit format. A hook blocks titles that do not.
- Assignee is the human whose git identity is on the commits. No reviewers unless the human names them.
- Label: exactly one, taken from the branch prefix through the table in `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 2. A prefix with no row in that table is a gap; ask before raising.
- Description: what, why, how to test, risks and rollback. Link sources instead of restating them.
- Merge: squash-and-merge. The reviewer has the final call.
- `git push` and `gh pr create` always ask before running. That is intended.
# Working agreement

How this team works with Claude Code. Applies to every session in this repo.

- Write in plain English: chat, docs, commit messages, PR text, code comments. Short sentences. If a simpler word carries the same meaning, use it.
- Lead with the answer or the outcome. Supporting detail comes after; leave out steps that do not change what the reader does next. Bullets for parallel items.
- Plan, align, execute. For anything beyond a small change, state the approach in a few lines and get a yes before building. Ask when different readings of the task would lead to different work. Do not ask about routine choices.
- Estimate in agent-pair time, not human-solo time. A well-aligned agent and human pair finishes in roughly a twentieth of the solo-human time. Give estimates as bounded work ("4 file edits, 1 migration, 1 PR" or "within a session"), never as human days. Name external waits (CI, deploys, reviews) separately.
- At the start of a session, run `/repo-sync` before writing code. Never switch or pull a repo that has uncommitted work without saying so.
- Stay in scope. Change only what the task names. Unrelated problems become a one-line follow-up note, not an inline fix.
- When a written plan or spec and the situation disagree, stop and ask. Never deviate silently, even when the deviation looks like an improvement. The spec for this repo is `docs/kickoff.md`, then the plan docs in `docs/plans/`.
- Report outcomes as they are. Failing tests are reported as failing, with output. Skipped steps are named. "Done" means `/verify` passed.
- The session transcript is shared with the reviewers as the record of how AI was used. Do the work inside the session: run the red test, then the green one, where the transcript shows both. Keep the human's decisions and the agent's work easy to tell apart.
- Keep the Claude Code files true to the code. Before a PR, `/claude-docs-check` reads the branch diff against `.claude/skills/claude-docs-check/map.json` and updates CLAUDE.md or the mapped rule on Opus, or records why not. A hook blocks `gh pr create` until that decision is on the branch.
- Before opening a PR, run `/raise-pr` and wait for a yes. One PR per branch.

- A fixture runs the backend suite in asyncio debug mode with a 50 ms slow-callback threshold and fails any test during which the event loop was blocked.
- The race tests and the load tests are run with the lead present: show the scripts and budgets first, then walk through the results.

## Mechanics
- Mock at the boundary (the HTTP client, `fetch`, the clock), never inside the code under test. Nothing in a unit suite opens a socket.
- Tests are independent and order-free. Each builds its own data through factories or fixtures; none relies on another's leftovers.
- Assert on behaviour a user or caller can see: status, body, rendered text and roles. Never on private attributes or CSS class names.
- One reason to fail per test. The name says the behaviour: `test_reorder_rejects_task_owned_by_another_user`, `it("shows the empty state when the user has no tasks")`.
- Coverage is a floor, not a target: CI fails below the threshold set in `pyproject.toml` and `vitest.config.ts`. A line covered by a test that asserts nothing is not covered.
- Report results as they are. "128 passed" means you saw it. Name the suite and the stack it ran against.
# Coding standards

Applies to `backend/` (Python) and `frontend/` (TypeScript). The path-scoped rules add the language detail.

## General
- Minimal code. No speculative abstractions. No options nobody asked for.
- Concise but descriptive. A name says what a thing is or does; a reader should not need the comment to follow the code.
- Prefer editing an existing file to adding one. Delete what is unused. No dead branches.
- Every public function, class, component and type carries a one-line summary in the language's doc format (Google-style docstrings in Python, JSDoc in TypeScript). Sections (`Args:`, `@param`) only when they add something the signature does not say. Other comments are single line and only where the code cannot say it. No comment blocks. No commented-out code.
- Every change is verifiable. If you cannot test it, say so before shipping it.
- Match the surrounding code's style, not its gaps.

## Functional and declarative style (a hard requirement)
- Functional core, imperative shell. Domain logic (validation, ordering, search filters, mapping rows to responses) is pure functions with no I/O. Routers, repositories and React components are the thin shell that does I/O and calls the core.
- Never mutate an input. Return a new value. Python: frozen dataclasses, Pydantic models with `frozen=True` where they flow through the core, tuples over lists for fixed data. TypeScript: `const`, `readonly`, spread, `toSorted`/`toSpliced`/`with` over `sort`/`splice`.
- Prefer expressions to statements: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, comprehensions and generator expressions over loops that append into an accumulator. Use a loop only when it reads more clearly, and never just to mutate an outer variable.
- Compose small functions instead of writing one long one. Higher-order functions where they remove repetition: FastAPI `Depends` factories, decorators, hooks that take a query function, comparator builders. Do not add one for a single caller.
- Pick the data structure for the access pattern: a dict or `Map` for lookup by id, a set for membership, a list or tuple for order. Say why in review when it is not obvious.
- No hidden shared mutable state: no module-level caches that requests write to, no singletons holding request data.

## Async and concurrency (a hard requirement)
- Use the high-level abstraction, never hand-rolled threads or callbacks. Backend: `async def` handlers, the async SQLAlchemy session, `asyncio.TaskGroup` (or `gather`) when independent awaits can run together. Frontend: TanStack Query for all server state (caching, retries, cancellation, optimistic updates with rollback), never `useEffect` plus `fetch`.
- Never block the event loop. CPU-heavy work (password hashing) runs through `asyncio.to_thread` or the library's async API.

## Boundaries and types
- Every value that crosses a boundary (HTTP body, database row, token claims, storage, URL params) is a typed model, validated right after it is read: Pydantic in Python, Zod in TypeScript. Field access happens on the validated value. No `dict[str, Any]`, `any` or `Record<string, unknown>` for a known shape.
- Type hints on every parameter and return value, tests included. TypeScript is `strict`; no `any`, no `as unknown as`, no `@ts-ignore`.

## Logging
- Logs exist to monitor the running app and find bugs. Keep every line that does that: startup and ready, shutdown, a caught exception with its context, a request that failed auth or validation at WARNING, a degraded path taken.
- Remove every line added only to chase a bug during development before the commit. A log line that would not help someone on call is noise.
- Backend: `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)`, never `print`. Frontend: `console.info` for lifecycle, `console.warn` and `console.error` for failures; never `console.log` or `console.debug`. ESLint enforces the frontend list.
- WARNING and ERROR lines say where, why and what happens next, with ids as key=value (`user_id=`, `task_id=`, `request_id=`). Never log secrets, passwords, tokens or full request bodies.

## Hygiene
- No `TODO`, `FIXME`, `XXX` or `HACK` in code. A follow-up goes in the PR description or an issue.
- No `debugger`, `breakpoint()`, `pdb`, or focused tests (`.only`). `python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py` checks all of this and runs in CI and in `/verify`.
- Secrets never appear in code, logs, tests, or chat. `.env` files and key material are off limits; a hook enforces this. Anything bundled into the frontend is public.
# Git and pull requests

## Branches
- Work on a branch off `main`: `feature/<name>`, `fix/<name>`, `chore/<name>`, `docs/<name>`, `refactor/<name>`, `perf/<name>`, `test/<name>`, `ci/<name>`. Lowercase, hyphens, no personal names.
- Never commit on `main`. Never force-push a shared branch. Never `--no-verify`. A hook blocks all three.
- Releases are `vX.Y.Z` tags on `main`. A tag is never moved or deleted; a wrong tag is fixed by cutting the next version. A hook blocks tag moves.

## Commits
- One logical change per commit, and every commit is green (see `testing.md`). Conventional Commits: `type(scope): subject`. Types: feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor, perf, test, ci, build, revert, release. Scopes: `api`, `web`, `db`, `auth`, `deploy`, `claude`, or none. Subject starts lowercase, no trailing period, imperative mood.
- The body says why, not what.
- Add `Refs: #<issue>` or `Refs: docs/plans/<file>.md` when there is one.

## Pull requests
- Run `/raise-pr`. It shows the card (title, branch, base, assignee, label, summary) and waits for a yes.
- The title follows the commit format. A hook blocks titles that do not.
- Assignee is the human whose git identity is on the commits. No reviewers unless the human names them.
- Label: exactly one, taken from the branch prefix through the table in `CONTRIBUTING.md` § 2. A prefix with no row in that table is a gap; ask before raising.
- Description: what, why, how to test, risks and rollback. Link sources instead of restating them.
- Merge: squash-and-merge. The reviewer has the final call.
- `git push` and `gh pr create` always ask before running. That is intended.
# Working agreement

How this team works with Claude Code. Applies to every session in this repo.

- Write in plain English: chat, docs, commit messages, PR text, code comments. Short sentences. If a simpler word carries the same meaning, use it.
- Lead with the answer or the outcome. Supporting detail comes after; leave out steps that do not change what the reader does next. Bullets for parallel items.
- Plan, align, execute. For anything beyond a small change, state the approach in a few lines and get a yes before building. Ask when different readings of the task would lead to different work. Do not ask about routine choices.
- Estimate in agent-pair time, not human-solo time. A well-aligned agent and human pair finishes in roughly a twentieth of the solo-human time. Give estimates as bounded work ("4 file edits, 1 migration, 1 PR" or "within a session"), never as human days. Name external waits (CI, deploys, reviews) separately.
- At the start of a session, run `/repo-sync` before writing code. Never switch or pull a repo that has uncommitted work without saying so.
- Stay in scope. Change only what the task names. Unrelated problems become a one-line follow-up note, not an inline fix.
- When a written plan or spec and the situation disagree, stop and ask. Never deviate silently, even when the deviation looks like an improvement. The spec for this repo is `docs/kickoff.md`, then the plan docs in `docs/plans/`.
- Report outcomes as they are. Failing tests are reported as failing, with output. Skipped steps are named. "Done" means `/verify` passed.
- The session transcript is shared with the reviewers as the record of how AI was used. Do the work inside the session: run the red test, then the green one, where the transcript shows both. Keep the human's decisions and the agent's work easy to tell apart.
- Keep the Claude Code files true to the code. Before a PR, `/claude-docs-check` reads the branch diff against `.claude/skills/claude-docs-check/map.json` and updates CLAUDE.md or the mapped rule on Opus, or records why not. A hook blocks `gh pr create` until that decision is on the branch.
- Before opening a PR, run `/raise-pr` and wait for a yes. One PR per branch.

# Contributing to `todo-app`

This file is the canonical reference for *how* we work in this repo. The *why* (requirements, architecture, design decisions) lives in `docs/`: start with `docs/kickoff.md`.

> **TL;DR for first-time contributors:** branch off `main`, use Conventional Commits, run the tests before opening a PR, get one reviewer, squash-merge.

---

## 1. Branches and merges

```
feature/<name>      ←  you work here, branched off main
       │
       │  GATE — every suite passes on this branch (§ 5)
       ▼
       PR  →  main   ←  squash-merged after review
       │
       ▼
   vX.Y.Z tag       ←  a release is a tag on main; a tag is never moved or deleted
```

**Never push directly to `main`.** Always go through a PR. A wrong tag is fixed by cutting the next version, never by moving the existing one.

Deployment moves through three stages, each proven before the next starts: containers with `docker compose`, then a local k3d cluster, then AKS through GitHub Actions. `.claude/rules/deployment.md` holds the details. Rollback on Kubernetes is `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>`, run by a human (§ 11).

## 2. Branch naming and PR labels

- Lowercase with hyphens. No spaces, no underscores, no camelCase, no personal names.
- Prefix with type. Short and descriptive: what the branch *does*, not who is doing it.

✓ Good: `feature/task-reorder` · `fix/token-expiry-401` · `docs/readme-deploy`
✗ Bad:  `my-branch` · `Fix-Login-Alex` · `main-2` · `feature/everything`

Every PR carries exactly one label, taken from its branch prefix:

| Branch prefix | Label |
|---|---|
| `feature/` | `enhancement` |
| `fix/` | `bug` |
| `docs/` | `documentation` |
| `chore/` | `chore` |
| `refactor/` | `refactor` |
| `perf/` | `performance` |
| `test/` | `test` |
| `ci/` | `ci` |

A prefix that is not in this table is a gap: add a row in the same PR, after asking.

## 3. Commit messages — Conventional Commits

```
type(scope): short description in imperative mood, ≤ 72 chars

Optional body wrapped at 72, explaining *why* not *what*.

Refs: #123 — link the issue, discussion or plan doc when there is one
Co-Authored-By: <the agent's attribution line, when an agent wrote it>
```

Types: `feat` · `fix` · `refactor` · `perf` · `chore` · `docs` · `test` · `ci` · `build` · `revert` · `release`

Example: `feat(search): add hybrid ranking for short queries`

## 4. Pull requests

Use the template:

```markdown
## What
One paragraph: what does this PR do?

## Why
Link the issue, discussion or plan doc when there is one.

## How to test
Step-by-step. Reviewer should be able to verify in < 5 min.

## Risks / rollback
What could break? How to revert?

## Screenshots / logs
Inline if helpful.
```

- One reviewer minimum. Two for changes touching production paths.
- CI must be green before merge.
- **Squash-merge** to `main`. History stays readable; every change has one review record.

## 5. Test gates

**Before every commit and before opening a PR**, from the repo root, for each part the change touched:

```bash
python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py                                     # no task markers, debuggers, focused tests or debug-only logs
cd backend && uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check . && uv run mypy && uv run pytest
cd frontend && npm run check && npm run test && npm run build         # ESLint + Prettier + tsc, Vitest, Vite build
```

Changes to the running stack also run the live-server e2e and Playwright suites against it. `.claude/rules/testing.md` says which layer owns which behaviour.

If a gate is red, fix it on the branch. Do not commit and do not open the PR.

## 6. Stashing work-in-progress safely

```bash
git stash push -u -m "wip on hybrid search, schema half-done"
#                ↑  -u = also stash *untracked* files (new files you haven't `git add`-ed)
git stash list
git stash apply stash@{0}        # safer than `pop` if you're uncertain
```

Three rules: always include `-m`, always include `-u`, pop on the same branch you stashed from.

## 7. Working with Claude Code

This repo is set up to be paired with Claude Code. `CLAUDE.md` is what the agent reads first; `.claude/rules/` carries the topic rules; `.claude/skills/` carries the workflows.

The session shape:

1. `/repo-sync` before writing code.
2. Plan, align, execute. For anything beyond a small change the agent states the approach and waits for a yes.
3. `/verify` before saying done.
4. `/claude-docs-check`, then `/raise-pr`, which shows a card and waits for a yes.

Useful prompts:

- `"Create a new branch off main called feature/<name> and switch to it."`
- `"Stage and commit my changes with a Conventional Commits message. Type is fix, scope is api, refs issue #42."`
- `"Sync my branch with origin/main, rebase, resolve conflicts conservatively and ask before discarding anything."`
- `"Before doing anything that touches main, follow CONTRIBUTING.md § 8 (the kind-stop protocol)."`

## 8. The kind-stop protocol — when you're about to break a rule

We expect **every coding agent** working in this repo (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, custom agents, future agents we haven't named yet) to follow this protocol when a human or another agent asks for something that would violate the rules in this file.

The goal is **not** to block the work. The goal is to **catch the deviation early**, explain it without condescension, and offer a path that gets the same outcome through the right channel. Everyone is at a different point on the git learning curve. We assume good faith in every request and we keep the warnings short, kind, and useful.

For Claude Code specifically, mechanical enforcement runs via the hooks in `.claude/hooks/` — see § 8.4.

### 8.1 What counts as a stop-and-warn event

Any of these in a single session:

1. Committing directly on `main` (no feature branch)
2. Pushing directly to `main` (no PR)
3. Force-pushing to a shared branch (`main`, anything someone else might be on)
4. Using a personal-name or vague branch name (`<name>-fix`, `claude-update`, `tmp`, `wip`, `update`, `fix`)
5. Skipping the test gate before opening a PR
6. Using `--no-verify` to bypass a git hook
7. Squashing the commits on a PR branch before merge (squash happens *on merge*, not before)
8. Moving, deleting or re-creating a release tag
9. Editing files in any folder marked "generated" or "source — do not modify"
10. A commit message that isn't Conventional Commits format
11. Opening a PR without the standard template (What / Why / How to test / Risks)
12. Deleting a branch that has unpushed commits or an open PR
13. Running `git reset --hard` or `git clean -fd` on a branch with uncommitted work the user might still want

If the agent is uncertain whether something is a violation, **treat it as one and ask**. A 30-second pause is cheaper than an irreversible mistake.

### 8.2 The pre-approved warning format

When an agent detects a stop-and-warn event, it pauses and outputs a message in **exactly this shape**. No deviation from the structure; predictability is what makes it useful.

```
⚠️  Heads up — this would deviate from CONTRIBUTING.md

What you asked for:
  <one sentence, neutral, no judgment>

Why I'm pausing:
  This would <specific rule violated> — see CONTRIBUTING.md § <number>.
  <One sentence on why the rule exists, in plain language.>

What I'd suggest instead:
  1. <concrete next step>
  2. <concrete next step>
  3. <concrete next step>
  (This gets you the same outcome through the right channel.)

If you still want to proceed as originally asked:
  Reply "proceed anyway" and I'll do it. I'll note the deviation in the
  commit/PR description so the team has a record. No judgment — sometimes
  there's a reason the rule doesn't fit. Just want to make sure it's a
  conscious choice, not a slip.
```

### 8.3 Tone rules for the agent

- **Lead with the request, not the rule.** Restate what was asked in neutral words first, so the human knows they were heard.
- **No "you violated."** Use "this would deviate from" or "this is outside our usual flow." We're flagging the action, not the person.
- **No lectures.** One sentence on why the rule exists. If the human wants more, they'll ask.
- **Always offer a path forward.** A warning without an alternative is just an obstacle. The alternative steps must be concrete enough to copy-paste.
- **Always offer the override.** Rules exist for the 95% case. A new contributor on day one and a senior engineer mid-incident both deserve the same respect: flag it, then trust them to choose. Record the choice; don't argue it.
- **One warning per deviation.** Don't re-warn on the same deviation in the same session if the user has already chosen "proceed anyway." Re-warning becomes nagging, which kills trust in the warning system.
- **Soft language is fine. Vague language is not.** "This is a bit outside our usual flow" is friendly. "Hmm, maybe consider..." is unhelpful. Be kind *and* specific.

### 8.4 Mechanical enforcement (Claude Code hooks)

For Claude Code users, the rules above are enforced by hooks wired in `.claude/settings.json`:

| Hook | Event | Blocks |
|---|---|---|
| `branch-protection.py` | Bash | commits and pushes on `main` (any form, including `HEAD:main`), force pushes, `--no-verify`, chained `git checkout main && git commit`, moving or deleting a `vX.Y.Z` tag |
| `env-protection.py` | Bash | any command that names a `.env*` path |
| `secrets-protection.py` | Bash, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit | writes to key material and credential files, and Bash commands that print them (`cat`, `grep` without `-l/-c/-q`, `awk`, ...) |
| `pr-title.py` | Bash | `gh pr create` / `gh pr edit` with a title that is not Conventional Commits |
| `docs-check.py` | Bash | `gh pr create` when the branch touched a path in `.claude/skills/claude-docs-check/map.json` and carries no docs decision |
| `lint.py` | after Edit, Write | nothing; it reports lint findings on the changed lines back to the agent |
| `transcript-backup.py` | PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionEnd | compaction, when the transcript snapshot fails; it copies the session transcript to `.ai-transcripts/` and reports a rewritten transcript |

They do **not** catch:
- Anyone running git outside Claude Code (terminal, IDE git pane, GitHub Desktop)
- Other agents (Cursor, Copilot, Codex, Aider); each has its own hook system or none
- Edits to `.github/workflows/*.yml` (those need code review)

That's why this protocol stays in CONTRIBUTING.md: the hooks are the safety net for the Claude Code path; this section is the universal contract.

**Per-user override** for emergencies: set `"disableAllHooks": true` in `.claude/settings.local.json` (gitignored). Hook lists merge across settings files, so an empty `"hooks": {}` does not turn them off. This is a deliberate escape hatch, auditable in your local config, never committed.

### 8.5 When the agent should refuse outright (no override)

These are not negotiable, even with "proceed anyway":

- Pushing to `main` without a PR (it deploys)
- Force-pushing `main` (rewrites deployed history)
- Deleting `main`
- Committing files matching `.env*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*credentials*`, `*secrets*`, anything that smells like a secret. If the human insists, the agent should ask them to add the file to `.gitignore` first and stage only the non-secret parts.
- Running `rm -rf` on anything outside the repo, or on `.git/` itself

For these, the response is:

```
⛔  I can't do this one, even with "proceed anyway."

  <one-sentence reason — what specifically breaks>

  If you have an authorized exception (incident response, security rotation,
  approved by the team), please do this manually with full awareness of the
  blast radius. I'm not the right tool for this action.
```

### 8.6 How to invoke it

Humans don't need to invoke it; it's the default behavior. If you ever notice an agent *not* using this format on a deviation, that's a bug; flag it in the PR review and we'll fix the instructions.

If you're reviewing a PR and the description mentions `Deviation noted: <X>`, that means the contributor hit the warning, chose "proceed anyway," and the agent recorded it. Treat it as a normal review signal, not a flag, just context.

---

## 9. Working from a written plan — for agents (and humans pairing with them)

When an agent is implementing from a plan doc (the kind that lives in `docs/plans/`), three rules govern how it takes direction.

### 9.1 The three rules

1. **Plan contradictions = STOP and ask.** If a plan's main body says one thing and an open-question section recommends another, the agent must surface the contradiction and let the human lock the answer before coding. Open questions are open until a human locks them. A line labeled `Recommendation: ...` inside an unlocked Q&A section is *not* a default to silently follow; it's a candidate for the human's review.
2. **Default to replacement, not addition.** When a plan describes swapping element X for element Y, the agent ships a swap. *"Keep X as fallback alongside Y, gated by a flag"* is dual-path complexity sold as safety: it bloats the code, and creates branches that future readers and agents must reason about. Additive patterns require a **named, real failure mode** that justifies them, not a hypothetical "safety rail."
3. **Rollout ramps live in deploy config, not in the artifact.** Gradual rollout is an ops concern (env var, feature flag at the deploy boundary, canary release). It is not a reason to keep two parallel implementations inside one module. The artifact ships the new behavior as the only behavior; ops decides which version is live.

### 9.2 The warning format for plan contradictions (extends § 8.2)

```
⚠️  Heads up — this plan has a contradiction (or asks for an additive pattern)

What the plan says:
  Body §<N>: <quote>
  Open Q-<N>: <quote>

Why I'm pausing:
  These two recommendations point in different directions. CONTRIBUTING.md §9.1
  says open questions stay open until a human locks them, and that I should ask
  before silently picking a side.

What I'd suggest:
  1. Lock the open question now (drop X / keep X as fallback / replace X with Y)
  2. Update the plan doc to reflect the lock
  3. Then I'll implement against the locked spec

If you'd like me to proceed with one option without locking the plan first:
  Reply "proceed with <option>" — I'll note the deviation in the PR description.
```

---

## 10. Merge discipline — who can merge what to `main`

### 10.1 The merger's responsibility

Whoever clicks the merge button must, before clicking:

1. **Have written or read the code thoroughly.** File-by-file, line-by-line for the diff, not just the PR description. If the diff is too large to read in one sitting, ask the contributor to split it.
2. **Have tested it locally.** Pulled the branch, run it, exercised the changed paths. CI green is necessary but not sufficient.
3. **Confirm the test gate passed for real.** If a contributor said "tests pass" but the merger can't verify, the merger runs them again.

If any of the three is false, the PR doesn't merge yet.

### 10.2 Only stable tested code goes to `main`

- **Don't merge to "see if it works there."** That's what your local environment is for.
- **Don't merge to "unblock another PR."** Stack the branches instead.
- **Don't merge because "it's mostly done."** Mostly done isn't done.

### 10.3 If issues are found *after* merge, raise a NEW PR

Do not reopen the merged PR, force-push over the merged commit, amend it, or revert and recommit on the same branch. Raise a fresh `fix/...` branch off `main`, fix the issue, open a new PR, get it reviewed, merge.

The one exception is a critical regression that breaks `main` for everyone: there, a `git revert` PR (a NEW commit that undoes the merged one) is the right tool. Even then, the *fix* lands as a separate, reviewed PR after the revert.

---

## 11. Operational scripts and deployments — the human-runs-it rule

Operational scripts that touch live infrastructure (reindex, deploy, secret rotation, schema migration against a shared database, bucket sync) **run from a human's terminal, not from inside an agent session.** Agents prepare and document; humans execute.

The handoff an agent produces has five parts: what the script does, what it touches, the exact command, how to verify it worked, and how to roll it back. Put a "STOP — read before running" block at the top of each ops folder's README and each script's docstring; that is the in-flight trigger that fires when an agent reads the file before acting. Hooks cannot tell "mutates prod" from "reads prod"; this rule is the contract.

Every deployment artifact (Dockerfile, compose file, Kubernetes manifest, overlay, workflow) is reviewed by the human before it is applied or merged. The agent never applies anything to AKS or another shared cloud resource.

---

## 12. Secrets discipline — agents do not write or expose `.env` and friends

Secrets files (`.env`, `.env.*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.crt`, `*.p12`, `credentials.*`, `secrets.*`, `~/.ssh/*`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `.docker/config.json`, `.kube/config`, etc.) are **user-managed**, not agent-managed.

### 12.1 The three rules

1. **Agents never write, edit or append to secrets files via `Edit` / `Write` / `MultiEdit` / `NotebookEdit`.** Even when the agent has the new value (a freshly minted token), the *write* belongs to the user. The agent prints the proposed change as text; the user pastes it.
2. **Agents never read-and-print secrets files via Bash.** `cat .env`, `head .env`, `grep <pattern> .env`, `awk ... .env`, `xxd key.pem`, all blocked. The contents would land in the agent's context window and become exposable through transcript replay or compaction.
3. **Agents may write *scripts* that mutate secrets files, with one binding constraint: the script must not print secrets to stdout.** A `sed -i` that updates a token in place is fine. A script that opens `.env`, transforms it and writes back is fine *if* you've verified by reading it that nothing prints the value.

### 12.2 `.env.example` is human-owned too

The hooks and the deny list cover `.env.example` as well. When a change needs a new setting, the agent posts the exact lines for `.env.example` in chat and the human adds them. Do not loosen the hooks to let the agent write it.

### 12.3 Allowed patterns the hook still blocks

These don't expose contents, but `env-protection.py` blocks every Bash command that names a `.env*` path. Run them yourself, or add a one-off allow in `.claude/settings.local.json`:

- `ls -la .env`, `wc -l .env`, `chmod 600 .env`
- `grep -l`, `grep -q`, `grep -c` on `.env`
- `sed -i 's/^KEY=.*/KEY=<new>/' .env`
- `echo "NEW_KEY=value" >> .env` (append; the agent must not have read the existing contents)

For the wider set (`*.pem`, `credentials.*`, ...) `secrets-protection.py` blocks only the printing readers, so `ls`, `wc`, `chmod`, `grep -l/-q/-c` and `sed -i` pass.

### 12.4 What to do when the agent needs to update a secret

1. **Print the proposed change as text** in chat: *"replace line 41 with: `API_TOKEN=…`"*. The user makes the edit.
2. **Or write a `sed -i` command** that updates the value in place without reading the existing value back.
3. **Or write an external script** the user invokes themselves.

### 12.5 The warning format

Use the § 8.2 shape with the rule reference `CONTRIBUTING.md § 12 (Secrets discipline)` and the specific action ("write to .env" / "read-and-print key.pem") in the "Why I'm pausing" line.

- `secrets-protection.py` blocks Edit, Write, MultiEdit and NotebookEdit on the full pattern list, and Bash commands that print one of those files.

Not covered: a script the agent writes that prints a secret as a side effect. Rule 12.1.3 is the contract for that case.

## 13. Screenshot and log review — review several before reporting back

When a test run, a UI walkthrough or a log capture produces artifacts the agent must review before reporting status:

- Aggregate findings before responding. "10/10 captured" without a per-row issue list is a violation of this rule. Captured is not correct.

A "restart" can fail to bind the port because the old process still holds it; the new one exits silently and the test runs against stale code with the confidence of fresh evidence. Before any test that depends on a local server:

1. Kill the old process.
2. Confirm the port is free: `lsof -ti:<port>` returns nothing.
3. Start the new process.
4. Confirm the listener PID is the new one: `lsof -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN -P -n`.
5. Confirm the uptime matches your restart: `ps -o etime -p <new-pid>` shows seconds, not hours.
6. Confirm the application is serving: the startup line in the log, or a known endpoint.

# Contributing to `todo-app`

This file is the canonical reference for *how* we work in this repo. The *why* (requirements, architecture, design decisions) lives in `docs/`: start with `docs/kickoff.md`.

> **TL;DR for first-time contributors:** branch off `main`, use Conventional Commits, run the tests before opening a PR, get one reviewer, squash-merge.

---

## 1. Branches and merges

```
feature/<name>      ←  you work here, branched off main
       │
       │  GATE — every suite passes on this branch (§ 5)
       ▼
       PR  →  main   ←  squash-merged after review
       │
       ▼
   vX.Y.Z tag       ←  a release is a tag on main; a tag is never moved or deleted
```

**Never push directly to `main`.** Always go through a PR. A wrong tag is fixed by cutting the next version, never by moving the existing one.

Deployment moves through three stages, each proven before the next starts: containers with `docker compose`, then a local k3d cluster, then AKS through GitHub Actions. `.claude/rules/deployment.md` holds the details. Rollback on Kubernetes is `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>`, run by a human (§ 11).

## 2. Branch naming and PR labels

- Lowercase with hyphens. No spaces, no underscores, no camelCase, no personal names.
- Prefix with type. Short and descriptive: what the branch *does*, not who is doing it.

✓ Good: `feature/task-reorder` · `fix/token-expiry-401` · `docs/readme-deploy`
✗ Bad:  `my-branch` · `Fix-Login-Alex` · `main-2` · `feature/everything`

Every PR carries exactly one label, taken from its branch prefix:

| Branch prefix | Label |
|---|---|
| `feature/` | `enhancement` |
| `fix/` | `bug` |
| `docs/` | `documentation` |
| `chore/` | `chore` |
| `refactor/` | `refactor` |
| `perf/` | `performance` |
| `test/` | `test` |
| `ci/` | `ci` |

A prefix that is not in this table is a gap: add a row in the same PR, after asking.

## 3. Commit messages — Conventional Commits

```
type(scope): short description in imperative mood, ≤ 72 chars

Optional body wrapped at 72, explaining *why* not *what*.

Refs: #123 — link the issue, discussion or plan doc when there is one
Co-Authored-By: <the agent's attribution line, when an agent wrote it>
```

Types: `feat` · `fix` · `refactor` · `perf` · `chore` · `docs` · `test` · `ci` · `build` · `revert` · `release`

Example: `feat(search): add hybrid ranking for short queries`

## 4. Pull requests

Use the template:

```markdown
## What
One paragraph: what does this PR do?

## Why
Link the issue, discussion or plan doc when there is one.

## How to test
Step-by-step. Reviewer should be able to verify in < 5 min.

## Risks / rollback
What could break? How to revert?

## Screenshots / logs
Inline if helpful.
```

- One reviewer minimum. Two for changes touching production paths.
- CI must be green before merge.
- **Squash-merge** to `main`. History stays readable; every change has one review record.

## 5. Test gates

**Before every commit and before opening a PR**, from the repo root, for each part the change touched:

```bash
python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py                                     # no task markers, debuggers, focused tests or debug-only logs
cd backend && uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check . && uv run mypy && uv run pytest
cd frontend && npm run check && npm run test && npm run build         # ESLint + Prettier + tsc, Vitest, Vite build
```

Changes to the running stack also run the live-server e2e and Playwright suites against it. `.claude/rules/testing.md` says which layer owns which behaviour.

If a gate is red, fix it on the branch. Do not commit and do not open the PR.

## 6. Stashing work-in-progress safely

```bash
git stash push -u -m "wip on hybrid search, schema half-done"
#                ↑  -u = also stash *untracked* files (new files you haven't `git add`-ed)
git stash list
git stash apply stash@{0}        # safer than `pop` if you're uncertain
```

Three rules: always include `-m`, always include `-u`, pop on the same branch you stashed from.

## 7. Working with Claude Code

This repo is set up to be paired with Claude Code. `CLAUDE.md` is what the agent reads first; `.claude/rules/` carries the topic rules; `.claude/skills/` carries the workflows.

The session shape:

1. `/repo-sync` before writing code.
2. Plan, align, execute. For anything beyond a small change the agent states the approach and waits for a yes.
3. `/verify` before saying done.
4. `/claude-docs-check`, then `/raise-pr`, which shows a card and waits for a yes.

Useful prompts:

- `"Create a new branch off main called feature/<name> and switch to it."`
- `"Stage and commit my changes with a Conventional Commits message. Type is fix, scope is api, refs issue #42."`
- `"Sync my branch with origin/main, rebase, resolve conflicts conservatively and ask before discarding anything."`
- `"Before doing anything that touches main, follow CONTRIBUTING.md § 8 (the kind-stop protocol)."`

## 8. The kind-stop protocol — when you're about to break a rule

We expect **every coding agent** working in this repo (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, custom agents, future agents we haven't named yet) to follow this protocol when a human or another agent asks for something that would violate the rules in this file.

The goal is **not** to block the work. The goal is to **catch the deviation early**, explain it without condescension, and offer a path that gets the same outcome through the right channel. Everyone is at a different point on the git learning curve. We assume good faith in every request and we keep the warnings short, kind, and useful.

For Claude Code specifically, mechanical enforcement runs via the hooks in `.claude/hooks/` — see § 8.4.

### 8.1 What counts as a stop-and-warn event

Any of these in a single session:

1. Committing directly on `main` (no feature branch)
2. Pushing directly to `main` (no PR)
3. Force-pushing to a shared branch (`main`, anything someone else might be on)
4. Using a personal-name or vague branch name (`<name>-fix`, `claude-update`, `tmp`, `wip`, `update`, `fix`)
5. Skipping the test gate before opening a PR
6. Using `--no-verify` to bypass a git hook
7. Squashing the commits on a PR branch before merge (squash happens *on merge*, not before)
8. Moving, deleting or re-creating a release tag
9. Editing files in any folder marked "generated" or "source — do not modify"
10. A commit message that isn't Conventional Commits format
11. Opening a PR without the standard template (What / Why / How to test / Risks)
12. Deleting a branch that has unpushed commits or an open PR
13. Running `git reset --hard` or `git clean -fd` on a branch with uncommitted work the user might still want

If the agent is uncertain whether something is a violation, **treat it as one and ask**. A 30-second pause is cheaper than an irreversible mistake.

### 8.2 The pre-approved warning format

When an agent detects a stop-and-warn event, it pauses and outputs a message in **exactly this shape**. No deviation from the structure; predictability is what makes it useful.

```
⚠️  Heads up — this would deviate from CONTRIBUTING.md

What you asked for:
  <one sentence, neutral, no judgment>

Why I'm pausing:
  This would <specific rule violated> — see CONTRIBUTING.md § <number>.
  <One sentence on why the rule exists, in plain language.>

What I'd suggest instead:
  1. <concrete next step>
  2. <concrete next step>
  3. <concrete next step>
  (This gets you the same outcome through the right channel.)

If you still want to proceed as originally asked:
  Reply "proceed anyway" and I'll do it. I'll note the deviation in the
  commit/PR description so the team has a record. No judgment — sometimes
  there's a reason the rule doesn't fit. Just want to make sure it's a
  conscious choice, not a slip.
```

### 8.3 Tone rules for the agent

- **Lead with the request, not the rule.** Restate what was asked in neutral words first, so the human knows they were heard.
- **No "you violated."** Use "this would deviate from" or "this is outside our usual flow." We're flagging the action, not the person.
- **No lectures.** One sentence on why the rule exists. If the human wants more, they'll ask.
- **Always offer a path forward.** A warning without an alternative is just an obstacle. The alternative steps must be concrete enough to copy-paste.
- **Always offer the override.** Rules exist for the 95% case. A new contributor on day one and a senior engineer mid-incident both deserve the same respect: flag it, then trust them to choose. Record the choice; don't argue it.
- **One warning per deviation.** Don't re-warn on the same deviation in the same session if the user has already chosen "proceed anyway." Re-warning becomes nagging, which kills trust in the warning system.
- **Soft language is fine. Vague language is not.** "This is a bit outside our usual flow" is friendly. "Hmm, maybe consider..." is unhelpful. Be kind *and* specific.

### 8.4 Mechanical enforcement (Claude Code hooks)

For Claude Code users, the rules above are enforced by hooks wired in `.claude/settings.json`:

| Hook | Event | Blocks |
|---|---|---|
| `branch-protection.py` | Bash | commits and pushes on `main` (any form, including `HEAD:main`), force pushes, `--no-verify`, chained `git checkout main && git commit`, moving or deleting a `vX.Y.Z` tag |
| `env-protection.py` | Bash | any command that names a `.env*` path |
| `secrets-protection.py` | Bash, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit | writes to key material and credential files, and Bash commands that print them (`cat`, `grep` without `-l/-c/-q`, `awk`, ...) |
| `pr-title.py` | Bash | `gh pr create` / `gh pr edit` with a title that is not Conventional Commits |
| `docs-check.py` | Bash | `gh pr create` when the branch touched a path in `.claude/skills/claude-docs-check/map.json` and carries no docs decision |
| `lint.py` | after Edit, Write | nothing; it reports lint findings on the changed lines back to the agent |
| `transcript-backup.py` | PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionEnd | compaction, when the transcript snapshot fails; it copies the session transcript to `.ai-transcripts/` and reports a rewritten transcript |

They do **not** catch:
- Anyone running git outside Claude Code (terminal, IDE git pane, GitHub Desktop)
- Other agents (Cursor, Copilot, Codex, Aider); each has its own hook system or none
- Edits to `.github/workflows/*.yml` (those need code review)

That's why this protocol stays in CONTRIBUTING.md: the hooks are the safety net for the Claude Code path; this section is the universal contract.

**Per-user override** for emergencies: set `"disableAllHooks": true` in `.claude/settings.local.json` (gitignored). Hook lists merge across settings files, so an empty `"hooks": {}` does not turn them off. This is a deliberate escape hatch, auditable in your local config, never committed.

### 8.5 When the agent should refuse outright (no override)

These are not negotiable, even with "proceed anyway":

- Pushing to `main` without a PR (it deploys)
- Force-pushing `main` (rewrites deployed history)
- Deleting `main`
- Committing files matching `.env*`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*credentials*`, `*secrets*`, anything that smells like a secret. If the human insists, the agent should ask them to add the file to `.gitignore` first and stage only the non-secret parts.
- Running `rm -rf` on anything outside the repo, or on `.git/` itself

For these, the response is:

```
⛔  I can't do this one, even with "proceed anyway."

  <one-sentence reason — what specifically breaks>

  If you have an authorized exception (incident response, security rotation,
  approved by the team), please do this manually with full awareness of the
  blast radius. I'm not the right tool for this action.
```

### 8.6 How to invoke it

Humans don't need to invoke it; it's the default behavior. If you ever notice an agent *not* using this format on a deviation, that's a bug; flag it in the PR review and we'll fix the instructions.

If you're reviewing a PR and the description mentions `Deviation noted: <X>`, that means the contributor hit the warning, chose "proceed anyway," and the agent recorded it. Treat it as a normal review signal, not a flag, just context.

---

## 9. Working from a written plan — for agents (and humans pairing with them)

When an agent is implementing from a plan doc (the kind that lives in `docs/plans/`), three rules govern how it takes direction.

### 9.1 The three rules

1. **Plan contradictions = STOP and ask.** If a plan's main body says one thing and an open-question section recommends another, the agent must surface the contradiction and let the human lock the answer before coding. Open questions are open until a human locks them. A line labeled `Recommendation: ...` inside an unlocked Q&A section is *not* a default to silently follow; it's a candidate for the human's review.
2. **Default to replacement, not addition.** When a plan describes swapping element X for element Y, the agent ships a swap. *"Keep X as fallback alongside Y, gated by a flag"* is dual-path complexity sold as safety: it bloats the code, and creates branches that future readers and agents must reason about. Additive patterns require a **named, real failure mode** that justifies them, not a hypothetical "safety rail."
3. **Rollout ramps live in deploy config, not in the artifact.** Gradual rollout is an ops concern (env var, feature flag at the deploy boundary, canary release). It is not a reason to keep two parallel implementations inside one module. The artifact ships the new behavior as the only behavior; ops decides which version is live.

### 9.2 The warning format for plan contradictions (extends § 8.2)

```
⚠️  Heads up — this plan has a contradiction (or asks for an additive pattern)

What the plan says:
  Body §<N>: <quote>
  Open Q-<N>: <quote>

Why I'm pausing:
  These two recommendations point in different directions. CONTRIBUTING.md §9.1
  says open questions stay open until a human locks them, and that I should ask
  before silently picking a side.

What I'd suggest:
  1. Lock the open question now (drop X / keep X as fallback / replace X with Y)
  2. Update the plan doc to reflect the lock
  3. Then I'll implement against the locked spec

If you'd like me to proceed with one option without locking the plan first:
  Reply "proceed with <option>" — I'll note the deviation in the PR description.
```

### 10.1 The merger's responsibility

Whoever clicks the merge button must, before clicking:

1. **Have written or read the code thoroughly.** File-by-file, line-by-line for the diff, not just the PR description. If the diff is too large to read in one sitting, ask the contributor to split it.
2. **Have tested it locally.** Pulled the branch, run it, exercised the changed paths. CI green is necessary but not sufficient.
3. **Confirm the test gate passed for real.** If a contributor said "tests pass" but the merger can't verify, the merger runs them again.

If any of the three is false, the PR doesn't merge yet.

### 10.2 Only stable tested code goes to `main`

- **Don't merge to "see if it works there."** That's what your local environment is for.
- **Don't merge to "unblock another PR."** Stack the branches instead.
- **Don't merge because "it's mostly done."** Mostly done isn't done.

Do not reopen the merged PR, force-push over the merged commit, amend it, or revert and recommit on the same branch. Raise a fresh `fix/...` branch off `main`, fix the issue, open a new PR, get it reviewed, merge.

232	          WhyNothing is built twice: what you approve is the code that ships. Splitting views from containers also keeps the views pure functions of their props, which makes them easy to test and easy to explain.
233	          DirectionFrom the lead: a stellar look, a premium feel, vintage colours, zero redundancy.
234	          FlagThis puts the first frontend code before the instructions walkthrough. To keep that safe, it follows the coding standards from the first line, the views hold no data logic the walkthrough could change, component tests come in the same commits, and it stays on feature/web-design-system. Its PR waits until the walkthrough is done.
235	    Waits outside our control: about 2 minutes of CI per push, plus your review of each PR and of the design.
236	    Why round 1 is shaped this way
237	    What changes in rounds 2 and 3
238	    The images, the app code and the probes stay the same in all three rounds. Only what surrounds them changes, which is why round 1 already has one origin, a one-shot migration and two replicas.
239	         |  | Concern | Round 1 · compose | Round 2 · k3d | Round 3 · AKS
240	           | Front door | nginx in web | Traefik Ingress (built into k3d) | Managed ingress with TLS
241	           | API scale | 2 replicas | Deployment, 3 replicas, rolling updates | Same, plus a pod autoscaler
242	           | Database | Postgres container and volume | Postgres StatefulSet | Azure Database for PostgreSQL
243	           | Migrations | One-shot service | Job before rollout | Job, run by the workflow
244	           | Secrets | Env file the human creates | Kubernetes Secret the human creates | Key Vault through the CSI driver
245	           | Images | Built locally | Imported into k3d, tagged with the git sha | Azure Container Registry, pushed by GitHub Actions (OIDC sign-in, no stored keys)
246	           | Manifests | None | Kustomize base + k3d overlay | Same base + aks overlay
247	    Exit criteria
248	    Round 1 is done when
249	        It works
250	          On a clean Mac, docker compose up --build brings up the stack and localhost:8080 lets a new user sign up and use every feature.
251	          Two users never see each other's tasks, through the UI or the API.
252	          The layout holds at phone width and at desktop width.
253	        It's proven
254	          All five test layers are green and above the coverage floors; you've reviewed the code.
255	          The load test passes its budgets, every user's data checks out afterwards, and the round's capacity figure is recorded.
256	          CI runs hygiene, backend, frontend and end-to-end jobs once the GitHub remote exists.
257	          The README covers running round 1 on a Mac.
258	    Not in round 1
259	    Later, in FUTURE.md
260	      Sign-in with Microsoft, Google or Apple (OpenID Connect), chosen per client. Refresh-token rotation and revocation.
261	      AI task entry: describe a new task or a change in text or voice, and the app makes it. Only once everything else works.
262	      AI summary home page for the user's tasks, possibly built on the AG-UI protocol.
263	      Account care: email verification and password reset. Data care: a rank rebalancing job, and paging for long lists.
264	    Sign-off record
265	    Signed off
266	    D1 to D20 are locked. Revision 1 settled D3, D4, D6, D7, D8, D10 and D12. Revision 2's D13 to D20 were signed off on 2026-10-19, with these notes from the lead:
267	      D15: report realistic concurrent-user numbers at the end of each round, measured by the stepped load test.
268	      D16 and D18: the lead takes part in the race tests and the load tests.
269	      D17: a tab refreshes when the user comes back to it. Kept as the first layer, with the version check as the guarantee.
270	      Design: a stellar look, a premium feel, vintage colours and zero redundancy.
271	    The detailed coding plan (docs/plans/round-1.md) and the design artifact are now being written in parallel.
