todo-app Round 1 Spec
    todo-app · spec · revision 3 · signed off
    Round 1: the app, running in containers
    The high-level choices for the To Do app and how the pieces fit, before the detailed coding plan is written. Each choice names what it beat and what it costs. Every decision is now locked: revision 1 settled the product choices, and revision 2 added how the API behaves when many people use it at once. Revision 3 records the lead's sign-off and notes.
    2026-10-19 · revision 3Lives at docs/specs/round-1.htmlBuilds on docs/kickoff.mdLater ideas: FUTURE.md
      Round 1 · this specContainersdocker compose up on a Mac. Every suite green.
      Round 2Local k3dSame images, Kubernetes manifests, three API replicas.
      Round 3AKS liveAzure, deployed by GitHub Actions, if time permits.
      TopologyDecisionsOrderingBackend shapeConcurrencyRacesAPIDataScreensTestsOrder of workRounds 2 and 3Done meansLaterSign-off
    Solution diagram
    One origin, two API replicas, one database
    The browser only ever talks to web on port 8080. Nginx serves the built SPA and forwards /api/* to the API, so the app and the API share one origin: no CORS, and the session cookie stays first-party. Running two API replicas already in round 1 proves the backend keeps no state in memory, one round before Kubernetes depends on it.
        [svg]
      Round 1 runs four services. migrate uses the API image and must exit successfully before either replica starts, so no replica serves an old schema and replicas never race to migrate. The tests go through the same front door a user does.
    High-level choices
    Decisions
    Locked ones come from the kickoff or follow directly from it. The rest are recommendations for you to confirm.
      D1
        Stack
locked
          ChoiceBackend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy 2 async with asyncpg, alembic, uv, ruff, mypy strict. Frontend: React 19, Vite, TypeScript strict, React Router, TanStack Query 5, Zod, Tailwind 4, dnd-kit, ESLint and Prettier, npm.
          Instead ofNode and Express, which the brief gives as an example.
          WhyTyped models at every boundary on both sides, native async, and an OpenAPI document for free. TanStack Query is the high-level async layer the brief asks for on the frontend.
      D2
        Storage is PostgreSQL from day one
locked
          ChoicePostgres 17 in a container with a named volume. The same engine runs as a StatefulSet in round 2 and as Azure Database for PostgreSQL in round 3.
          Instead ofIn-memory or file storage, or SQLite.
          WhySeveral replicas must share one store, and transactions plus constraints keep reorder and ownership correct. Integration tests run on the same engine as production, so they test what ships.
      D3
        Accounts: open sign-up and sign-in by email
locked
          ChoiceThe landing page is sign-in, with a link to create an account (email and password, 12 to 128 characters). Passwords are hashed with argon2id, off the event loop.
          Instead ofSeeded demo users only, or a third-party login.
          WhyA reviewer can make two accounts and see that each one only sees its own tasks. Nothing to configure, and no outside service.
          CostsNo email verification or password reset in round 1; both are in FUTURE.md.
          AlsoReviewers can script bulk tests against the API: the OpenAPI document and interactive docs are served at /api/docs.
      D4
        Session: a signed token in an httpOnly cookie
locked
          ChoiceOn sign-in the API sets a JWT (HS256, 8-hour lifetime) as cookie session: HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/api, Secure once TLS exists in rounds 2 and 3. Sign-out clears it. Any replica can verify it with the shared secret.
          Instead ofA bearer token in localStorage, which any injected script can read. Or a sessions table, which can be revoked but adds a lookup per request.
          WhyStateless across replicas and out of reach of page scripts. CSRF is covered by SameSite=Strict, the single origin, JSON-only request bodies and an Origin check on every write.
          CostsA token can't be revoked before it expires. Refresh-token rotation with a deny list is the round 3 hardening item.
          LaterSign-in with Microsoft, Google or Apple (OpenID Connect), chosen per client. Recorded in FUTURE.md.
      D5
        Ids are UUIDs
locked
          ChoiceUsers and tasks use UUID primary keys generated by the API.
          Instead ofSerial integers.
          WhyIds can't be guessed or counted, and any replica can mint one without asking the database first.
      D6
        Ordering by fractional ranks
locked
          ChoiceEach task has a rank string, and the list is sorted by rank. A move computes a new rank between its new neighbours, so it changes one row. New tasks go to the top. Reordering is turned off while a search is active, because moving within a filtered subset is ambiguous.
          Instead ofInteger positions renumbered on every move, or gapped integers with occasional rebalancing.
          WhyOne write per move whatever the list size, no renumbering, and the rank maths is a pure function we can test with generated inputs (see the figure below).
          CostsRanks get longer when many tasks are dropped into the same gap. In practice that's a character or so per move into one spot; a rebalancing job goes on the "more time" list.
      D7
        Search runs on the server
locked
          ChoiceGET /api/v1/tasks?q= matches a case-insensitive substring in title or notes, keeps rank order, and is backed by a trigram index. The search box waits 250 ms after typing stops and keeps showing the previous results while the next ones load.
          Instead ofFiltering the loaded list in the browser.
          WhyThe API owns operations on the data, the index keeps search fast as lists grow, and paging can come later without changing how search behaves.
      D8
        Task fields
locked
          ChoiceTitle (required, 1 to 200 characters), notes (up to 5,000), completed, optional due date, created and updated times.
          Instead ofAlso priority, tags or subtasks.
          WhyThat's enough to make the detail screen worth opening, and every field gets tested end to end. More fields would add surface without showing anything new.
          LaterOnce everything works: create and update tasks by describing them in text or voice, and an AI-written summary home page, possibly over the AG-UI protocol. Recorded in FUTURE.md.
      D9
        HTTP contract
locked
          ChoiceResources under /api/v1. Success: 200, 201 with a Location header, 204. Errors: 400 for validation (FastAPI's 422 is remapped), 401 when the session is missing or bad, 403 when a write comes from another origin, 404 for a missing task or one owned by someone else, 409 when an email is already registered, 412 when an edit is based on an old version (D17), 503 when the API is overloaded or the database is unreachable (D13, D15). One error body shape: {"error": {"code", "message", "details"}}.
          WhyFollows the brief's status-code hint. Every code has a reason the frontend can act on. Answering 404 for other users' tasks means the API never confirms that someone else's id exists.
      D10
        Two API replicas already in round 1
locked
          ChoiceCompose runs api with two replicas, and nginx round-robins between them. Each response carries an X-Served-By header with the replica's hostname.
          Instead ofOne replica until round 2.
          WhyA live test can show that a session issued by one replica works on the other. Any accidental in-memory state shows up in round 1, where it's cheap to fix. The header also helps trace requests in Kubernetes.
      D11
        Logs for monitoring
locked
          ChoiceAPI logs are JSON lines on stdout. Each request gets one access line (request_id, user_id, method, route, status, duration_ms), plus a startup "ready" line and every caught error with context. X-Request-ID is accepted from the caller or created, and echoed back. /livez and /readyz are the probes (D19). In the SPA: console.info when it boots, and console.error from the error boundary and the global query error handler.
          WhyYour logging guidance: every line helps someone watching the system, and Kubernetes and Azure pick up stdout as is.
      D12
        Coverage floors
locked
          ChoiceCI fails below 90% line and branch coverage on the backend and 85% on the frontend. These are floors on tests that assert something, not targets to pad.
          WhyHigh enough that a missed branch shows up, low enough that nobody writes a pointless test just to cover glue code.
    D6 in one picture
    A move writes one row
    Moving “Buy milk” from the bottom to just below “Call Sam”. With integer positions, every task between the old and new place is renumbered. With ranks, only the moved task gets a new key, halfway between its new neighbours. Ranks compare byte by byte, so the column uses the "C" collation; a locale-aware collation would sort a0V in the wrong place.
        [svg]
      The API takes PUT /api/v1/tasks/{id}/position with {"after_id": … | null}. The server looks up the neighbours itself, inside one transaction, so a client with a stale view can't put a task between two tasks that are no longer next to each other.
    How a request moves
    Functional core, imperative shell
    Everything that touches the network or the database sits at the edges and stays thin. The rules (rank maths, the search pattern, applying a partial update, mapping rows to responses) are pure functions that never mutate their input, in a core that the unit tests reach directly. FastAPI's Depends composes each request from small providers. Errors are raised as domain exceptions and turned into HTTP status codes in one place.
        [svg]
      The shaded box is the only place business rules live, and nothing in it does I/O. Every repository query filters on owner_id, so ownership is enforced in the SQL itself, not checked after a row is loaded.
    Many users at once · FastAPI and uvicorn
    Async and concurrency
    Each API replica is one uvicorn process running one event loop. The loop can hold thousands of open requests, but only while each of them is waiting on I/O. Anything that keeps the loop busy (a slow hash, a blocking call, a synchronous write) stalls every request on that replica at once. So the design has three jobs: never block the loop, put a limit on every shared resource, and when a limit is reached, make requests queue for a bounded time or get a clear 503 rather than pile up.
        [svg]
      Everything the loop hands off has a limit: 200 requests in progress per replica, 15 database connections, 4 hashes at a time. When a limit is reached, requests wait for a bounded time; past that wait the client gets a 503 with the error envelope, never a hung connection.
      D13
        One uvicorn process per container, every handler async
locked
          Choiceuvicorn[standard] (uvloop, httptools) with one worker per container; more capacity means more replicas. Every route is async def and uses only async libraries. --limit-concurrency 200 answers 503 past 200 in-flight requests. --timeout-graceful-shutdown 20 lets in-flight requests finish on SIGTERM, then the lifespan closes the pool. Nginx keeps connections to the API open and caps request bodies at 64 KB.
          Instead ofGunicorn or uvicorn managing several worker processes inside one container. Or plain def handlers, which FastAPI runs on a thread pool capped at 40 threads by default.
          WhyOne process per container lets Docker and Kubernetes restart it, count it and scale it, and each pod's memory and CPU stay predictable. Async-only handlers mean the loop is the only scheduler to reason about.
      D14
        Password hashing runs off the loop, at most four at a time
locked
          Choiceargon2id with OWASP's parameters (19 MiB memory, 2 passes, 1 lane), run through asyncio.to_thread behind an asyncio.Semaphore(4) per process. argon2-cffi releases the GIL while it hashes, so the hashes really do run in parallel with the loop.
          Instead ofHashing on the loop, or without a limit.
          WhyOne hash takes tens of milliseconds of CPU. On the loop, every sign-in would freeze that replica for that long. Without a limit, a burst of sign-ins would exhaust memory: the library's default profile uses 64 MiB per hash, so 100 sign-ins at once would need over 6 GB. With the semaphore, extra sign-ins wait their turn instead.
      D15
        A connection budget, and timeouts on every wait
locked
          ChoiceAsync SQLAlchemy on asyncpg. Each replica has a pool of 10 connections plus 5 overflow, a 5-second wait for a free one, and pool_pre_ping. Postgres runs with statement_timeout 5 s and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout 10 s. Each request gets its own AsyncSession and one transaction, committed on success and rolled back on any exception. Sessions are never shared between concurrent coroutines, because an AsyncSession isn't safe for that.
          BudgetTotal connections = replicas × 15, kept under 80% of Postgres's 100. That's 30 in round 1 and 45 in round 2. Round 3 adds autoscaling, so it puts the PgBouncer built into Azure's Postgres in front.
          WhyRequests are short, so 15 connections serve many concurrent users. When load exceeds that, requests wait up to 5 seconds and then get a clear 503, rather than an unbounded queue taking down the database.
          ReportedThe final report states, for each round, how many concurrent users the stack served within budget, measured by D18 rather than estimated.
    Many requests touching the same rows
    Races and consistency
    Tasks are private, so two different users never contend for the same row. The races that remain come from one user (two tabs, fast drags, a double-click) and from users signing up with the same email. Every guard lives in Postgres, because a lock inside one Python process means nothing to the other replica.
        [svg]
      Both requests ask to place a task right after A. The shaded bars show who holds the per-user lock (pg_advisory_xact_lock on the owner id; it's released at commit). Without it, both would read a0 | a1 and both would write a0V. The unique index on (owner_id, rank) would then reject one, and the user would see an error instead of a silent tie. Other users' writes never wait for this lock.
      D16
        Order changes are serialized per user, in Postgres
locked
          ChoiceCreating a task and moving one each start their transaction with pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(owner_id::text, 0)), then read the neighbours, compute the rank and write. A unique index on (owner_id, rank) backs it up. Edits and deletes don't take the lock, since they never change ranks.
          IsolationPostgres's default, READ COMMITTED, and that's deliberate. Each statement reads a fresh snapshot, so the neighbour read after the lock is granted sees the other move's commit. Under REPEATABLE READ the snapshot would be taken at the lock statement, before that commit, and both moves would compute the same rank.
          Instead ofAn asyncio.Lock, which only covers one process. SERIALIZABLE everywhere, which needs retry loops on every write. A version check on the whole list.
          WhyThe lock is the narrowest correct one: one user's ordering writes queue for a few milliseconds, and nothing else waits.
          TestingThe race tests run with the lead present. We watch them fail with the lock removed, then pass with it in place, before the backend PR is raised.
      D17
        Tabs stay fresh, and edits can't silently overwrite each other
locked
          The caseTab 2 loaded a task before tab 1 saved a change to it. Tab 2 then saves its stale copy, and tab 1's change is silently lost.
          ChoiceTwo layers. First, freshness: whenever a tab regains focus or the network comes back, TanStack Query refetches what's on screen. If the refetch brings a newer version of a task while the user has unsaved edits to it, the detail screen says "Changed elsewhere" straight away and offers to review or reload. Second, the guarantee: each task has an integer version, sent as an ETag. PATCH with If-Match updates only if the version still matches (UPDATE … WHERE id = :id AND owner_id = :me AND version = :v), otherwise it returns 412. The detail screen always sends If-Match. PATCH changes only the fields sent.
          Why bothRefreshing on focus prevents most mismatches but can't catch them all. It mustn't overwrite a half-typed draft, a change from another device can land while this tab keeps focus, and scripted clients have no focus at all. The version check catches everything else in one conditional UPDATE, with no locks.
         |  | Race | Guard | Test that proves it
           | Two sign-ups with one email | Unique index on email; the insert's IntegrityError becomes 409. Never check-then-insert. | Integration: 20 concurrent sign-ups, exactly one 201 and nineteen 409s
           | Moves and creates in one list at once | Per-user advisory lock, unique (owner_id, rank) | Integration: 50 concurrent moves; afterwards the ranks are unique and the list holds the same tasks. Live: the same through both replicas
           | Two tabs edit one task | Refetch on focus; "Changed elsewhere" notice; version, If-Match, 412 | Integration: two PATCHes on the same version, one 200 and one 412. Component: a newer version arriving under a draft shows the notice
           | Edit or toggle after delete | Owner-scoped UPDATE affects 0 rows → 404 | Component: a 404 on a mutation removes the row and says why
           | A late search response overwrites a newer one | Results cached per search term; superseded requests aborted with AbortSignal | Hook test: MSW delays the response for "ab" past the one for "abc", and "abc" stays on screen
           | A refetch lands on top of an optimistic reorder | cancelQueries before the optimistic write; reorder mutations share one scope, so they run in order | Component: three quick moves end in the order the user made
           | Something blocks the event loop | Async-only handlers, hashing off the loop (D13, D14) | Backend fixture: asyncio debug mode with a 50 ms slow-callback threshold; a test fails if any callback blocks longer
           | Load beyond the limits | Request, connection and hash limits; 503 with the envelope (D13 to D15) | Load test (D18): no 5xx at target load, p95 within budget
      D18
        A load test before submission
locked
          Choicek6, run from its official container as a compose profile (docker compose --profile load run k6), so nothing needs installing. 200 virtual users, each with its own account, ramp up over 1 minute and hold for 3. Each one loops: list, search, create, toggle, move, edit, delete, with 1 second of think time. After the run, a check script confirms every user's list has unique ranks and the expected number of tasks.
          PassUnder 0.1% failed requests and no 5xx. p95 latency under 250 ms for reads and under 400 ms for writes; under 1.5 s for sign-in, which queues on purpose (D14). Results are saved with the machine's specs and quoted in the README.
          Instead ofLocust, which is Python and fits the backend, but lacks k6's built-in pass/fail thresholds.
          WhyIt shows the limits in D13 to D16 working under real concurrency, and gives reviewers a script they can rerun at their own scale.
          CapacityA second, stepped run raises the number of users until a budget breaks. The last step that passed is the round's capacity figure for the final report (D15). It's repeated in rounds 2 and 3.
          Run withThe lead. Scripts and budgets are reviewed before the first run, and results are walked through together.
    How we explain it in the deep-dive
      One request, end to end: every log line carries request_id, user_id, duration_ms and the replica that served it, so a single slow or failed request can be followed across both replicas.
      Each race has a test with the race in its name, from the table above, and each one fails if its guard is removed.
      The load test summary (throughput, p95 per endpoint, error rate, the consistency check) goes in the README next to this section's diagrams.
    Contract
    Endpoints
    Every write also returns 403 if its Origin doesn't match the app, and every task endpoint returns 401 without a valid session. Those two codes aren't repeated in each row below.
         |  | Method and path | Does | Success | Errors
           | POST /api/v1/auth/register | Create an account and sign in | 201 | 400, 409
           | POST /api/v1/auth/login | Sign in; sets the session cookie | 200 | 400, 401
           | POST /api/v1/auth/logout | Clear the session cookie | 204 | none
           | GET /api/v1/auth/me | Who is signed in | 200 | 401
           | GET /api/v1/tasks?q= | List own tasks in rank order, optionally searched | 200 | 400
           | POST /api/v1/tasks | Create a task at the top | 201 | 400
           | GET /api/v1/tasks/{id} | Read one task | 200 | 404
           | PATCH /api/v1/tasks/{id} | Change any of title, notes, completed, due date; honours If-Match | 200 | 400, 404, 412
           | PUT /api/v1/tasks/{id}/position | Move after another task, or to the top | 200 | 400, 404
           | DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{id} | Delete a task | 204 | 404
           | GET /api/docs · /api/openapi.json | Interactive API docs and the OpenAPI document, for scripting | 200 | none
           | GET /livez | Liveness: the process is up and its loop answers. Checks no dependencies. | 200 | none
           | GET /readyz | Readiness: SELECT 1 within 1 s, and not shutting down | 200 | 503
      D19
        Health checks: /livez and /readyz
locked
          ChoiceTwo probes at the API root, outside /api/v1. Nginx doesn't route them, so only Docker and Kubernetes reach them. Liveness checks nothing but the process. Readiness checks the database and starts failing as soon as shutdown begins.
          Instead of/health, or a single /healthz.
          WhyNo standard path exists: the IETF's health-check format never went past a draft. The trailing z is Google's convention for keeping probe paths clear of app routes. Kubernetes deprecated /healthz for its own API server in v1.16 in favour of separate /livez and /readyz, and we follow that split. Keeping them separate matters: if liveness checked the database, a short database outage would make Kubernetes restart every API pod at once, turning a blip into an outage. Readiness only takes a pod out of rotation.
    List responses are wrapped as {"items": [...]}, so a paging cursor can be added later without breaking the client. An after_id that doesn't exist and one that belongs to someone else get the same 400, so the response doesn't reveal which it was.
    Schema
    Two tables
         |  | Table | Columns | Constraints and indexes
           | users | id uuid · email citext · password_hash text · created_at timestamptz | Primary key on id; email unique, compared case-insensitively
           | tasks | id uuid · owner_id uuid · title varchar(200) · notes text · completed bool · due_date date null · rank text collate "C" · version integer · created_at, updated_at timestamptz | owner_id references users, delete cascades; unique index (owner_id, rank); trigram GIN index on title and notes; checks on title and notes length
    Frontend
    Screens
         |  | Route | Screen | Notes
           | /sign-in | Landing: sign in | Link to sign-up. After sign-in, goes back to the page that asked for it.
           | /sign-up | Create account | Errors shown next to each field, checked by the same Zod schema the API layer uses.
           | /tasks | Task list | Search box, quick add at the top, a checkbox on each row, drag by mouse, touch or keyboard. Empty, loading and error states.
           | /tasks/:id | Task detail | View and edit every field, save, and delete with a confirm step built into the page. Shows "Changed elsewhere" when a newer version arrives under unsaved edits.
           | * | Not found | Also shown for a task id that isn't yours.
      Responsive: one column from 320 px wide, a centred reading width on desktop, and 44 px touch targets.
      Server data lives only in TanStack Query. Toggle, reorder and delete update the screen immediately, roll back on error and show what failed. Create and edit wait for the server and show progress.
      Expired session: a 401 on any request clears the cache and goes to sign-in with a return path, handled once in the query client.
    Each layer earns its place
    Tests
    Each behaviour is tested once, at the lowest layer that can catch it. Red, then green, inside the session. Every commit is green.
         |  | Layer | Tool | Owns | Runs against
           | Backend unit | pytest, Hypothesis | Rank maths (property-based), search pattern escaping, patch application, token and password helpers | Nothing; pure functions
           | Backend integration | pytest, httpx ASGI transport, asyncio.TaskGroup | Every endpoint's success and error codes, response shapes, ownership, persistence, the 422-to-400 mapping, the concurrent races above, and that Postgres sorts ranks the same way Python does | A real Postgres (the compose db; a service container in CI)
           | Frontend unit and component | Vitest (Jest's API), React Testing Library, MSW | Helpers, hooks, and each screen's states, optimistic rollback, field errors | jsdom, with fetch mocked at the boundary
           | Live API | pytest, httpx | Migrations ran, the proxy and cookie path work, a session from one replica works on the other, deep links serve the SPA, security headers are set | The compose stack on :8080
           | Browser end to end | Playwright | Four journeys: sign up and sign in; create, edit, complete; reorder and search; delete and sign out. Plus one at phone size | The compose stack on :8080
           | Load | k6 (container) | Throughput, latency and error budgets with 200 concurrent users, and data consistency afterwards (D18) | The compose stack on :8080, before submission
    Sequence
    Order of work: design before frontend code
      You sign off this spec.
      In parallel: the detailed coding plan (docs/plans/round-1.md), and a design artifact showing the tokens and every screen in every state.
      Gate: you review the design tokens and the screens. Changes go into the tokens and components, and the artifact is republished.
      Gate: the walkthrough of the coding instructions, with code, comment-style and type-checking samples.
      PRs, each reviewed by you after the card: skeleton, spec and plan, backend API, frontend (connecting the reviewed screens to real data), then containers with the live, browser and load tests.
      Gate: round 1 is done (below), then round 2.
      D20
        The design artifact is built from the real components
locked
          ChoiceTokens go in frontend/src/styles/tokens.css as Tailwind 4 @theme variables (colour, type, spacing, radius, motion, light and dark). Building blocks go in frontend/src/components/ui/. Each screen is a view that takes its data and callbacks as props and does no fetching. A second Vite entry, frontend/design/, renders the token sheet and every view in every state with sample data, at phone and desktop widths.   - "backend/app/main.py"
  - "backend/tests/integration/**"

# API contract

The REST contract between `backend/` and `frontend/`. Change both sides in the same PR, or neither.

- Resources are nouns under `/api/v1`: `/auth/...`, `/tasks`, `/tasks/{id}`. Standard methods: `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PATCH` updates part of a resource, `DELETE` removes. JSON in and out.
- Status codes:

| Case | Code |
|---|---|
| Read or update succeeded | 200 |
| Created; the response carries the resource and a `Location` header | 201 |
| Deleted | 204, no body |
| Body or query fails validation | **400** (FastAPI's default is 422; the app maps `RequestValidationError` to 400 in one handler) |
| No token, bad token, expired token, wrong password | 401 |
| Authenticated but not allowed to do this action | 403 |
| Resource missing, **or owned by another user** (so ids of other users' tasks are never confirmed) | 404 |
| Conflict with current state, such as an email already registered | 409 |
| `If-Match` names an old version of the task | 412 |
| Overloaded (in-flight limit, no free database connection) or database unreachable | 503 |

- JSON field names are camelCase on the wire (`dueDate`, `createdAt`). Pydantic models use `alias_generator=to_camel` with `populate_by_name=True`; Python code keeps snake_case.
- Tasks carry an integer `version`, returned as the `ETag` header. `PATCH` honours `If-Match` (412 on mismatch) and changes only the fields sent.
- Every error body has one shape, a typed model: `{"error": {"code": "...", "message": "...", "details": [...]}}`. `code` is a stable machine string the frontend switches on; `message` is safe to show a user.
- List endpoints return a typed envelope, not a bare array, so paging can be added without breaking clients.
- The frontend parses every response with a Zod schema that mirrors the backend's Pydantic model. When a model changes, the schema changes in the same PR, and the integration test for that endpoint asserts the new shape.
- Every endpoint has an integration test for its success code and each error code it can return.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail when shipped code carries task markers, debugger hooks, focused tests or debug-only logging."""

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path, PurePosixPath

PathFilter = Callable[[PurePosixPath], bool]

ROOTS = ("backend", "frontend", "e2e", "deploy")
TEXT_SUFFIXES = frozenset(
    {
        ".py",
        ".ts",
        ".tsx",
        ".js",
        ".jsx",
        ".mjs",
        ".css",
        ".html",
        ".yml",
        ".yaml",
        ".toml",
        ".cfg",
        ".ini",
        ".sh",
    }
)
SKIP_PARTS = frozenset(
    {
        "node_modules",
        ".venv",
        "dist",
        "build",
        "coverage",
        "playwright-report",
        "test-results",
    }
)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Check:
    """One forbidden pattern and the files it applies to."""

    label: str
    pattern: re.Pattern[str]
    applies: PathFilter


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Hit:
    """One line that failed a check."""

    label: str
    path: PurePosixPath
    line_no: int
    line: str


def suffix_in(*suffixes: str) -> PathFilter:
    """Build a filter that accepts paths with one of the given suffixes."""
    return lambda path: path.suffix in suffixes


def under(prefix: str) -> PathFilter:
    """Build a filter that accepts paths below the given folder."""
    return lambda path: path.is_relative_to(prefix)


def all_of(*filters: PathFilter) -> PathFilter:
    """Combine filters so a path must pass every one."""
    return lambda path: all(f(path) for f in filters)


def negate(f: PathFilter) -> PathFilter:
    """Invert a filter."""
    return lambda path: not f(path)


is_python = suffix_in(".py")
is_script = suffix_in(".ts", ".tsx", ".js", ".jsx", ".mjs")


def is_test(path: PurePosixPath) -> bool:
    """True for backend tests and frontend `*.test.*` or `*.spec.*` files."""
    return (
        under("backend/tests")(path) or ".test." in path.name or ".spec." in path.name
    )


CHECKS = (
    Check("task marker", re.compile(r"\b(TODO|FIXME|XXX|HACK)\b"), lambda _: True),
    Check("python debugger", re.compile(r"\bbreakpoint\(|\bpdb\b"), is_python),
    Check(
        "print in backend code (use logging)",
        re.compile(r"^\s*print\("),
        all_of(is_python, negate(is_test)),
    ),
    Check("javascript debugger", re.compile(r"\bdebugger\b"), is_script),
    Check(
        "debug-only console call (use console.info, warn or error)",
        re.compile(r"\bconsole\.(log|debug|trace)\("),
        is_script,
    ),
    Check(
        "focused test",
        re.compile(r"\b(it|test|describe)\.only\("),
        all_of(is_script, is_test),
    ),
)


def repo_root() -> Path:
    """Return the top of the git work tree."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "rev-parse", "--show-toplevel"],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        check=True,
    ).stdout
    return Path(out.strip())


def candidate_files(root: Path) -> list[PurePosixPath]:
    """List tracked and untracked, non-ignored text files under the code roots."""
    out = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "ls-files", "--cached", "--others", "--exclude-standard", "--", *ROOTS],
        cwd=root,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        check=True,
    ).stdout
    paths = (PurePosixPath(line) for line in out.splitlines())
    return sorted(
        {
            p
            for p in paths
            if p.suffix in TEXT_SUFFIXES and SKIP_PARTS.isdisjoint(p.parts)
        }
    )


def scan(root: Path, path: PurePosixPath, checks: Iterable[Check]) -> Iterator[Hit]:
    """Yield every line in one file that fails a check that applies to it."""
    applicable = tuple(c for c in checks if c.applies(path))
    if not applicable:
        return
    try:
        lines = (root / path).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    except (OSError, UnicodeDecodeError):
        return
    yield from (
        Hit(c.label, path, n, line.strip())
        for n, line in enumerate(lines, start=1)
        for c in applicable
        if c.pattern.search(line)
    )


def main() -> int:
    """Scan the repo and print each hit; return 1 when there is any."""
    root = repo_root()
    hits = [hit for path in candidate_files(root) for hit in scan(root, path, CHECKS)]
    for hit in hits:
        print(f"{hit.path}:{hit.line_no}: {hit.label}: {hit.line}")
    print(
        f"hygiene check {'failed' if hits else 'passed'}: {len(hits)} finding(s)",
        file=sys.stderr if hits else sys.stdout,
    )
    return 1 if hits else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

content.text:
## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Pin every library URL to an exact version (`react@18.3.1` on jsDelivr or unpkg, `react/18.3.1/…` on cdnjs, `cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17`), never a bare name, a range or a tag (`react`, `react@18`, `@latest`). Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#key=value` state and never the query string — so deep-link to a tab or section with a bare token and keep all other state in the page.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

content.content:
# TypeScript

- `strict` is on in `tsconfig.json`. No `any`, no `as unknown as`, no `@ts-ignore`, no non-null `!` to silence a real `undefined`. Named exports. Function components with hooks; no classes.
- Every boundary is a Zod schema under `src/lib/schema/`: API responses, form data, storage, URL params. `parse`, or `safeParse` with a typed error path, right after reading; field access on the parsed value. Types come from the schema with `z.infer`, never written twice.
- Every API call goes through the one fetch wrapper in `src/lib/api/`, which attaches the token, parses the body and turns error bodies into a typed `ApiError`. No bare `fetch` in components or hooks.
- Domain types live in `src/types/` or next to their schema, reachable from any layer. Never define a cross-cutting type inside `components/`.
- Enums are `as const` objects, not `enum`. Use the typed constant, never the string literal.
- Discriminated unions are closed. Switch on the discriminant, and make the switch exhaustive with a `never` check.

python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py && git add frontend && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(web): add design tokens drawn from a bookkeeper's ledger

The lead asked for vintage colours from one real source, a premium
feel and zero redundancy. Every colour, size, radius, shadow and
duration now lives in tokens.css. The default Tailwind theme is
cleared, so a utility off the scale (p-5, bg-red-500) never
generates.

Each colour holds its light and dark value in one light-dark() pair,
so the palette is written once. The root's color-scheme picks the
value under the contracted selectors: light on :root, dark under the
guarded prefers-color-scheme query and under data-theme="dark".
Reduced motion zeroes the two duration tokens, so every transition
calms down from one place.

A test parses tokens.css and checks every text pairing at 4.5:1 and
every control pairing at 3:1 in both themes, and that every colour
has a documented role. The gallery's token sheet reads the same
module.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.content:
# React

- Function components with hooks. Every hook is declared before any conditional `return`; hooks run in the same order every render. `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` and `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` are errors.
- Server state lives in TanStack Query, and only there. Each resource has one module of query keys and hooks (`useTasks`, `useUpdateTask`); components never build query keys inline. Mutations that the user should see at once (reorder, toggle, delete) are optimistic, roll back on error and show the error.
- `useState` is for local affordances only: an open menu, a draft form value. Auth state is one context. Never copy server data into local state.
- Derive, do not mirror. A value computed from props or query data is computed during render (with `useMemo` only when it is measurably costly), never stored by an effect. `useEffect` is for syncing with something outside React, not for data flow.
- Forms validate with the same Zod schema the API layer uses, and show errors next to the field.
- Responsive by default, mobile first: Tailwind utilities, layouts that work from 320px wide up, touch targets of at least 44px, reorder that works by touch and by keyboard as well as by mouse.
- Accessible by default: real buttons and links, a label on every input, visible focus, and roles and names that tests query by.
- Styling: Tailwind utilities first. Inline `style` only for values the utility layer cannot express.

python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py && git add frontend && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(web): build the task list view from ledger primitives

The task list is the screen the lead reviews first, so it lands with
every state the spec implies: loading, empty, load error, ready,
searching with and without matches, reordering off while searching
(D6), a pending create, and a rolled-back action with a retry.

The view is props in, JSX out: no fetching, no router hooks, every
intent leaves as a callback, and moves leave as
onMove(taskId, afterId | null) to match PUT /position. Only the
quick-add draft is local state, validated by the same titleSchema
the API layer uses. Container queries (@wide) drive the layout, so
the view lays out by the width it is given. The same code renders
correctly in a 390px gallery frame and in the app.

Primitives cover what the screen needs and nothing more: button,
link (plain clicks navigate in the app, modified clicks stay with
the browser), text field, tick box, search box, notice, empty state,
skeleton, task row and a sortable list. The sortable list uses
dnd-kit's mouse, touch (press and hold) and keyboard sensors, one
per input, with move announcements in plain English. Its keyboard
test drives real Space, arrow, Space moves through dnd-kit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline -1

input.message:
## Phase 1 checkpoint: stopped for the lead's direction review

Phase 1 is committed and green, with nothing pushed and no PR. The scaffold, tokens, the primitives the list needs, `TaskListView` in every state, the gallery and screenshots are all in. The direction is a **bookkeeper's ledger**. Phase 2 waits for the go-ahead.

**Branch and commits**
Branch `feature/web-design-system`, on the local `docs/round-1-spec` tip (5caf53d), since no remote branches exist yet.

| sha | subject |
|---|---|
| 21874fb | chore(web): scaffold the frontend toolchain with the task schema |
| 2460e2c | feat(web): add design tokens drawn from a bookkeeper's ledger |
| 632bc99 | feat(web): add task list helpers and shared fixtures |
| f37e00e | feat(web): build the task list view from ledger primitives |
| 03c3f16 | fix(web): align placeholder rows and fit notices at phone width |
| 4f97dae | feat(web): add the design gallery built from the real views |
| 94cc9c1 | docs(web): add gallery screenshots for the direction review |

**Tests** (last run on HEAD, Vitest with jsdom)
- **96 tests passed** in 12 files.
- **Coverage:** lines 98.56% (137/139), branches 93.89% (123/131), statements 98.72%, functions 100%. The floor is 85%.
- `npm run check` (ESLint, Prettier, tsc), `npm run build` and the hygiene script all pass.
- Red then green is in the transcript for every unit. I split the primitives from the view and checked each commit's tree separately, so every commit is green on its own.

**Direction**
1. **Source:** mid-century American account ledgers and columnar pads. Pale green "eye-ease" paper, feint blue ruling, a red double margin rule, blue-black ink, a bottle-green cloth binding stamped in gilt.
2. **Palette:** light mode is the open page, dark mode is the closed binding, where the main action turns gilt. Red is only the margin rule and alert ink, so an overdue date is the one thing that shouts. The 13 colour tokens are canvas, sheet, ink, ink-muted, rule, rule-strong, margin, alert, primary, primary-strong, on-primary, focus and shade.
3. **Contrast:** every pairing meets WCAG AA in both themes. Text runs from 5.35:1 to 14.39:1, controls and focus from 3.37:1 up. A test fails the build if any pairing drops.
4. **Type:** Besley (a Clarendon revival) for headings only; Libre Franklin (a Franklin Gothic revival) for everything else, with tabular figures for dates. Both are self-hosted through @fontsource.
5. **Feel:** every row sits on a ruled line right of the red margin, with due dates in their own ruled column on wide screens. A 4px spacing grid plus a 44px touch step, corners of 2px and 4px, two shadows by role, 120ms and 220ms motion that drops to zero under reduced motion.

**Screenshots**
They are in `frontend/design/screenshots/`, 16 PNGs at 1x (4.9 MB). Each of overview, direction, tokens and task-list is shot at 390 and 1280, light and dark. I reviewed 2x crops of every state, and the page never scrolls sideways at either width.

The artifact is built to `frontend/design/dist/artifact.html` (599 KB). It is gitignored, so `npm run design:build` regenerates it, and I haven't published it.

**Decisions the brief didn't settle**
- **One `light-dark()` pair per colour.** Each colour is written once with its light and dark value side by side. The contracted selectors (`:root`, the guarded media query, `[data-theme="dark"]`) only switch `color-scheme`, so the dark palette isn't written twice. Tailwind's build polyfills `light-dark()`; switching at the root works, but a single element can't be themed on its own.
- **The default Tailwind theme is cleared.** Utilities off the scale (`p-5`, `bg-red-500`) simply don't exist.
- **Container queries instead of media queries.** The views respond to the width they're given, so a 390px gallery frame shows the real phone layout through the same component.
- **Sensors are mouse, touch (150ms press and hold) and keyboard,** one per input. A `PointerSensor` would claim every touch first and leave a `TouchSensor` doing nothing.
- **A `Link` primitive with a `NavigationProvider`** keeps the router out of views: plain clicks navigate in the app, modified clicks stay with the browser.
- **The search debounce belongs to the container.** The view is controlled by `query` and receives `searchPending`.
- **A create failure appears in the generic `failure` notice with a retry,** not as its own row state.
- **Dates use the `en-US` format** ("Overdue · Fri, Oct 16"), the page carries a dated overline, and notes are a non-null string, empty when there are none.
- **TypeScript is pinned to 6.0.3,** because typescript-eslint supports versions below 6.1.
- **The app entry `src/main.tsx` is a stub** until the router and data layer arrive.

**Folded in from the planner and your clarification**
- The CSP applies to the app build only. It emits external JS, CSS and font files, and nothing injects `<style>` tags at runtime.
- The schema rules match: title trimmed and 1 to 200 characters, notes up to 5,000, and moves sent as `onMove(taskId, afterId | null)`.
- `ErrorView` is noted for phase 2.

**Weaknesses**
- **The desktop frames are mostly empty canvas,** because the spec calls for a centred reading width. The phase 2 app shell should give that space a frame.

Phase 1 is committed and green, with nothing pushed and no PR. The scaffold, tokens, the primitives the list needs, `TaskListView` in every state, the gallery and screenshots are all in. The direction is a **bookkeeper's ledger**. Phase 2 waits for the go-ahead.

**Branch and commits**
Branch `feature/web-design-system`, on the local `docs/round-1-spec` tip (5caf53d), since no remote branches exist yet.

| sha | subject |
|---|---|
| 21874fb | chore(web): scaffold the frontend toolchain with the task schema |
